newsitem.title: FRANCE: National Front fizzles in French house election.
newsitem.headline: National Front fizzles in French house election.

text.p: French far-right leader Jean-Marie Le Pen said on Sunday after a leftist upset victory in a parliamentary election that France was headed towards ruin and held out his National Front as its saviour.
But the party's weak showing in the runoff vote undermined his plea. Only one Front candidate won a seat in the National Assembly, just one better than before.

"Behind the misleading appearances, the nation has been weakened, its independence has been weakened, its economic, social and diplomatic forces ruined by plans for Europeanisation. We must change paths, for things can only get worse," Le Pen said in a post-election statement.
He appealed to all "healthy parties" to join hands with the Front in reshaping France's political landscape, "to define and bring about a new politics that is popular, social and national".
But Le Pen acknowledged that just one of his party's candidates, Toulon mayor Jean-Marie Le Chevallier, had triumphed in his southern constituency.

Le Pen had earlier predicted that his xenophobic party, which wants to ship home millions of immigrants and reserve jobs and state benefits for native-born French people, could win up to 20 seats, enough to form a political group in parliament and serve as a base for later expansion.
The Front's strong 14.94 percent score in last Sunday's first-round ballot had stunned mainstream parties. It had won 12.41 percent in 1993 legislative elections.

The party was able to place candidates in 132 of France's 577 constituencies in Sunday's runoff vote, a remarkable figure seen by analysts as a sign that the Front was now a major force in all French elections.

Le Pen boasted that Front voters would play a decisive role in the second-round runoffs, supporting only candidates who endorsed its anti-European stance and its plan to reserve jobs, education, housing and welfare for native-born French citizens.
But pollsters said his endorsements had scant impact.
The final tally was all the more disappointing for the Front as Le Pen himself did not stand in the election and his top two lieutenants failed to win seats.
Bruno Megret and Bruno Gollnisch, both of whom have been openly manoeuvring to succeed the 68-year-old Le Pen if and when he steps down as party leader, each lost in their southern French districts.
Strangely their losses bolstered Le Pen's standing within the party. Victories by Megret and Gollnisch would have marked the first steps towards a new generation of Front leadership.

But the losses also raised questions about Le Pen's strategy. He had initially called for a defeat of the governing centre-right, arguing that a leftist victory would lead to gridlock and new parliamentary or presidential elections.
But he had to change his tune after confused party militants complained that they favoured neither a rightist nor a leftist victory but a win by the Front itself.
In the final days of the campaign, Le Pen demonstrated why he has been so successful in keeping the National Front in the public eye but also why he remains a pariah in mainstream political circles.

On Friday, the fiery former paratrooper threw a female Socialist candidate to the ground and shouted obscenities at protesters during a campaign brawl in a Paris suburb where his daughter was standing for election.

The night before, he had paraded around the stage at a Paris campaign rally carrying an oversized photograph of the head of Socialist Strasbourg mayor Catherine Trautmann, set on a platter. The Socialist Trautmann had led an anti-Front protest in her eastern city two months ago.
